lec05kp17-u01-p1-title.name: u01-p1-title
lec05kp17-u01-p1-title.text: Polynomials, sigmoid nets and RBF are all universal approximators: the difference is how fast, not whether

lec05kp17-u01-p1-bridge.name: u01-p1-bridge
lec05kp17-u01-p1-bridge.text: The RBF of KP16 fills the space with local nodes. Which kind of new coordinates can finally approximate any function, and which does it fastest?

lec05kp17-u01-p1-fig1.name: fig:lec05-kp17-summary
lec05kp17-u01-p1-fig1.text: Three universal approximators: polynomials (error about r^(−2/l)), a one-hidden-layer sigmoid network (about 1/k) and an RBF network (also universal).

image.alt: Three universal approximators: polynomials (error about r^(−2/l)), a one-hidden-layer sigmoid network (about 1/k) and an RBF network (also universal).

lec05kp17-u01-p1-term:通用近似定理.name: term:Universal approximation theorem
lec05kp17-u01-p1-term:通用近似定理.text: **Universal approximation theorem**: with enough nodes (or a high enough order) any continuous function on a compact set can be approximated to any small error. A compact set is bounded and contains its boundary, for example the interval $[0,1]$.

lec05kp17-u01-p1-c1.name: u01-p1-c1
lec05kp17-u01-p1-c1.text: **All three hold**: polynomials (Weierstrass's theorem), a one-hidden-layer sigmoid network and an RBF network. Symbols: $l$ inputs, $r$ order, $k$ nodes.

lec05kp17-u01-p1-c2.name: u01-p1-c2
lec05kp17-u01-p1-c2.text: **The real difference**: how fast the error falls with the order, $O(r^{-2/l})$ against $O(1/k)$, and how hard the optimization is.

lec05kp17-u01-p2-title.name: u01-p2-title
lec05kp17-u01-p2-title.text: Polynomials approximate any continuous function: for sin 2πx + 0.3x² the largest error is only 0.000015 at r=9

lec05kp17-u01-p2-bridge.name: u01-p2-bridge
lec05kp17-u01-p2-bridge.text: All three are universal approximators. Polynomials first: does the error really keep falling as the order grows?

lec05kp17-u01-p2-fig1.name: fig:lec05-kp17-polyerr
lec05kp17-u01-p2-fig1.text: Semi-log curve of the polynomial largest error against the degree 1 to 12 for sin 2πx + 0.3x²: 0.0152 at r=5 and 0.000015 at r=9.

image.alt: Semi-log curve of the polynomial largest error against the degree 1 to 12 for sin 2πx + 0.3x²: 0.0152 at r=5 and 0.000015 at r=9.

lec05kp17-u01-p2-c1.name: u01-p2-c1
lec05kp17-u01-p2-c1.text: **Weierstrass's theorem**: for a continuous $g$ on a compact set and any $\epsilon>0$ there is an order-$r$ polynomial $\phi$ with $|g-\phi|<\epsilon$.

lec05kp17-u01-p2-c3.name: u01-p2-c3
lec05kp17-u01-p2-c3.text: **Note**: the largest error is the worst point of the whole interval, not an average; orders $2m-1$ and $2m$ tie since the even part is just $t^2$ plus a constant.

lec05kp17-u01-p3-title.name: u01-p3-title
lec05kp17-u01-p3-title.text: A high order is not always good: Runge interpolation has error 3.66 at r=12

lec05kp17-u01-p3-bridge.name: u01-p3-bridge
lec05kp17-u01-p3-bridge.text: The largest error of the polynomial fell steadily with the order. Is a higher order always a better fit?

lec05kp17-u01-p3-fig1.name: fig:lec05-kp17-runge
lec05kp17-u01-p3-fig1.text: The Runge function with two degree-12 polynomials: equal-spaced interpolation oscillates wildly at the ends (error 3.66) and least squares fits well (0.068).

image.alt: The Runge function with two degree-12 polynomials: equal-spaced interpolation oscillates wildly at the ends (error 3.66) and least squares fits well (0.068).

lec05kp17-u01-p3-term:龍格現象.name: term:Runge phenomenon
lec05kp17-u01-p3-term:龍格現象.text: **Runge phenomenon**: interpolating (forcing the polynomial through every sample point) a high-order polynomial through equal-spaced points oscillates wildly near the ends and the error grows.

lec05kp17-u01-p3-c1.name: u01-p3-c1
lec05kp17-u01-p3-c1.text: **Example**: $g=1/(1+25x^2)$ on $[-1,1]$; equal-spaced interpolation at $r=4,8,12,16,20$ has largest error $0.44,\,1.05,\,3.66,\,14.4,\,59.8$.

lec05kp17-u01-p3-c2.name: u01-p3-c2
lec05kp17-u01-p3-c2.text: **Contrast**: least squares on 400 points: $0.33,\,0.15,\,0.068,\,0.031,\,0.014$ at $r=4,8,12,16,20$, slow but steady.

lec05kp17-u01-p4-title.name: u01-p4-title
lec05kp17-u01-p4-title.text: A one-hidden-layer sigmoid network approximates too: k=2 nodes already give largest error 0.014

lec05kp17-u01-p4-bridge.name: u01-p4-bridge
lec05kp17-u01-p4-bridge.text: The polynomial needs least-squares coefficients and a high order needs care. With one hidden layer of sigmoids, how does the largest error depend on the number of nodes?

lec05kp17-u01-p4-fig1.name: fig:lec05-kp17-mlpfit
lec05kp17-u01-p4-fig1.text: The target wave with fits by k=1, 2 and 4 sigmoid nodes: k=1 is too flat, while k=2 and 4 nearly coincide with the target.

image.alt: The target wave with fits by k=1, 2 and 4 sigmoid nodes: k=1 is too flat, while k=2 and 4 nearly coincide with the target.

lec05kp17-u01-p4-term:擠壓函數.name: term:Squashing function
lec05kp17-u01-p4-term:擠壓函數.text: **Squashing function**: a monotonically increasing function that squeezes any input into a bounded range, for example the sigmoid.

lec05kp17-u01-p4-c1.name: u01-p4-c1
lec05kp17-u01-p4-c1.text: **Theorem**: with a squashing activation a one-hidden-layer network $\phi(x)=\sum_jw_j^of(w_j^{hT}x)+w_o^o$ with large enough $k$ approximates any continuous function on a compact set to any error.

lec05kp17-u01-p4-c2.name: u01-p4-c2
lec05kp17-u01-p4-c2.text: **Example** (the target of page 2): $k=1,2,3,4,6,8$, best of 8 random starts: largest error $0.819,\,0.0142,\,0.0056,\,0.0058,\,0.0045,\,0.0011$.

lec05kp17-u01-p5-title.name: u01-p5-title
lec05kp17-u01-p5-title.text: On a smooth one-dimensional target the polynomial is as good or better at equal parameters

lec05kp17-u01-p5-bridge.name: u01-p5-bridge
lec05kp17-u01-p5-bridge.text: The sigmoid network with $k=2$ has largest error 0.014. Against a polynomial with the same number of parameters, which is more accurate?

lec05kp17-u01-p5-fig1.name: fig:lec05-kp17-equal
lec05kp17-u01-p5-fig1.text: Largest error of polynomials and sigmoid networks at equal parameters (7, 13, 19): the polynomial is as good or better.

image.alt: Largest error of polynomials and sigmoid networks at equal parameters (7, 13, 19): the polynomial is as good or better.

lec05kp17-u01-p5-c1.name: u01-p5-c1
lec05kp17-u01-p5-c1.text: **7 parameters**: the polynomial $r=6$ gives $0.0152$ and the sigmoid network $k=2$ ($3k+1=7$) gives $0.0142$, about the same.

lec05kp17-u01-p5-c2.name: u01-p5-c2
lec05kp17-u01-p5-c2.text: **13 parameters**: the polynomial $r=12$ gives $2.5\times10^{-7}$ and the network $k=4$ gives $0.0058$.

lec05kp17-u01-p5-c3.name: u01-p5-c3
lec05kp17-u01-p5-c3.text: **So**: the advantage of the network is not on a smooth one-dimensional target; the rate difference of the theorem shows only in high dimensions (next page).

lec05kp17-u01-p6-title.name: u01-p6-title
lec05kp17-u01-p6-title.text: High dimension, a target that favours the net: one node nearly exact, 252 polynomial terms err 0.257

lec05kp17-u01-p6-bridge.name: u01-p6-bridge
lec05kp17-u01-p6-bridge.text: In one dimension the polynomial does not lose. With 5 inputs, who is more accurate?

lec05kp17-u01-p6-fig1.name: fig:lec05-kp17-ridge
lec05kp17-u01-p6-fig1.text: A 5-dimensional single-ridge target: polynomials r=1, 2, 3, 5 have errors 0.326, 0.326, 0.222, 0.257 on new points while networks k=1, 2, 4 are all below 0.0001.

image.alt: A 5-dimensional single-ridge target: polynomials r=1, 2, 3, 5 have errors 0.326, 0.326, 0.222, 0.257 on new points while networks k=1, 2, 4 are all below 0.0001.

lec05kp17-u01-p6-c1.name: u01-p6-c1
lec05kp17-u01-p6-c1.text: **Setup** (designed here): $l=5$ standard-normal inputs, target $\tanh(2w^Tx)$ (a sigmoid-type function of one direction $w$), 3000 training and 2000 new points, root-mean-square error.

lec05kp17-u01-p6-c3.name: u01-p6-c3
lec05kp17-u01-p6-c3.text: **Networks** $k=1,2,4$ (8, 15, 29 parameters): all below $0.0001$. **Note**: the target has exactly the shape of the network, a design that favours it.

lec05kp17-u01-p7-title.name: u01-p7-title
lec05kp17-u01-p7-title.text: The rates in the source: O(r^(−2/l)) for polynomials and O(1/k) for sigmoid networks, with no l in the latter

lec05kp17-u01-p7-bridge.name: u01-p7-bridge
lec05kp17-u01-p7-bridge.text: In high dimension the polynomial loses and one node is nearly exact. What are the error rates behind this?

lec05kp17-u01-p7-fig1.name: fig:lec05-kp17-halving
lec05kp17-u01-p7-fig1.text: Growth needed to halve the error: a polynomial's r times 2^(l/2) (2, 5.7, 32, 1024 for l=2, 5, 10, 20) against only doubling k for the network.

image.alt: Growth needed to halve the error: a polynomial's r times 2^(l/2) (2, 5.7, 32, 1024 for l=2, 5, 10, 20) against only doubling k for the network.

lec05kp17-u01-p7-c1.name: u01-p7-c1
lec05kp17-u01-p7-c1.text: **Rates** (Barron 93, source): $O(r^{-2/l})$ for polynomials and $O(1/k)$ for a one-hidden-layer sigmoid network, with the input dimension $l$ absent from the formula.

lec05kp17-u01-p7-c2.name: u01-p7-c2
lec05kp17-u01-p7-c2.text: **Example**: halving the error multiplies the polynomial's $r$ by $2^{l/2}$: $2,\,5.7,\,32,\,1024$ times for $l=2,5,10,20$; the network's $k$ only doubles.

lec05kp17-u01-p7-c3.name: u01-p7-c3
lec05kp17-u01-p7-c3.text: **Limit**: worst-case asymptotic rates, not measurements; a smooth target like page 2 can go much faster, and $r$ against $k$ is not parameter-by-parameter.

lec05kp17-u01-p8-title.name: u01-p8-title
lec05kp17-u01-p8-title.text: The reason is the basis: fixed for polynomials, data-adaptive for networks; the price is non-convexity

lec05kp17-u01-p8-bridge.name: u01-p8-bridge
lec05kp17-u01-p8-bridge.text: In the rate formulas the network has no dimension and the polynomial does. Why is the gap so large, and what is the price?

lec05kp17-u01-p8-fig1.name: fig:lec05-kp17-restarts
lec05kp17-u01-p8-fig1.text: Eight random starts on the same data: for k=2, 5 are below 0.1 and 3 are stuck near 0.82; k=3 also has stuck starts.

image.alt: Eight random starts on the same data: for k=2, 5 are below 0.1 and 3 are stuck near 0.82; k=3 also has stuck starts.

lec05kp17-u01-p8-term:固定基底.name: term:Fixed basis
lec05kp17-u01-p8-term:固定基底.text: **Fixed basis**: basis functions such as $x_1^2x_2$ that are the same whatever the data look like; polynomials use them.

lec05kp17-u01-p8-term:資料自適應基底.name: term:Data-adaptive basis
lec05kp17-u01-p8-term:資料自適應基底.text: **Data-adaptive basis**: basis functions $f(w^Tx)$ whose $w$ is optimized from the data; the hidden nodes of a network are such.

lec05kp17-u01-p8-c1.name: u01-p8-c1
lec05kp17-u01-p8-c1.text: **The price**: the optimization turns from linear into nonlinear. For the same data, $k=2$ with 8 random starts: 5 reach a largest error below 0.1 and 3 get stuck near 0.82 (program).

lec05kp17-u01-p9-title.name: u01-p9-title
lec05kp17-u01-p9-title.text: Extension: n stacked hat functions have 2^n pieces; one layer needs 2^n − 1 nodes

lec05kp17-u01-p9-bridge.name: u01-p9-bridge
lec05kp17-u01-p9-bridge.text: The price is non-convexity. If one hidden layer suffices, why use more layers?

lec05kp17-u01-p9-fig1.name: fig:lec05-kp17-hat
lec05kp17-u01-p9-fig1.text: The hat function stacked 1, 2, 3 times has 2, 4, 8 pieces; the table lists 6, 12, 20 nodes for a deep network and 7, 63, 1023 for one layer at n=3, 6, 10.

image.alt: The hat function stacked 1, 2, 3 times has 2, 4, 8 pieces; the table lists 6, 12, 20 nodes for a deep network and 7, 63, 1023 for one layer at n=3, 6, 10.

lec05kp17-u01-p9-c1.name: u01-p9-c1
lec05kp17-u01-p9-c1.text: **The hat function**: $h(x)=2\min(x,1-x)$ takes 2 ReLU nodes (the piecewise-linear activation $\max(0,x)$; same principle as the sigmoid); stacking $n$ layers gives $2^n$ straight pieces, counted by a program for $n=1..4$: 2, 4, 8, 16.

lec05kp17-u01-p9-c2.name: u01-p9-c2
lec05kp17-u01-p9-c2.text: **Number of nodes**: $2n$ when deep; a one-hidden-layer ReLU network has at most $k+1$ pieces and needs $2^n-1$ nodes. For $n=3,6,10$: 6, 12, 20 deep against 7, 63, 1023 in one layer.

lec05kp17-u01-p9-c3.name: u01-p9-c3
lec05kp17-u01-p9-c3.text: **The source says**: more than one hidden layer may reach the same accuracy with fewer neurons.

lec05kp17-u01-p10-title.name: u01-p10-title
lec05kp17-u01-p10-title.text: Extension: practice, the cost of halving the error and a five-fold hat function

lec05kp17-u01-p10-bridge.name: u01-p10-bridge
lec05kp17-u01-p10-bridge.text: Stacking $n$ hat functions saves many nodes in a deep network over one layer. With the same kind of counting, how much must $r$ grow to halve the error at $l=8$, and how many nodes does a five-fold hat function need?

lec05kp17-u01-p10-q1.name: u01-p10-q1
lec05kp17-u01-p10-q1.text: **Question 1**: $l=8$ and the polynomial error $\sim r^{-2/l}$. By what factor must $r$ grow to halve the error?

lec05kp17-u01-p10-q2.name: u01-p10-q2
lec05kp17-u01-p10-q2.text: **Question 2**: how many pieces does the five-fold hat function $h(h(h(h(h(x)))))$ have, and how many ReLU nodes do a deep network and a one-hidden-layer network need?

lec05kp17-u01-p11-title.name: u01-p11-title
lec05kp17-u01-p11-title.text: Extension: worked solution of questions 1 and 2

lec05kp17-u01-p11-bridge.name: u01-p11-bridge
lec05kp17-u01-p11-bridge.text: The practice asked for the cost of halving the error and of the five-fold hat function. Worked out in full, what are the answers?

lec05kp17-u01-p11-a2.name: u01-p11-a2
lec05kp17-u01-p11-a2.text: **Question 2**: 5 layers have $2^5=32$ pieces; the deep network needs $2\times5=10$ nodes and one hidden layer needs $2^5-1=31$.

lec05kp17-u01-p11-a3.name: u01-p11-a3
lec05kp17-u01-p11-a3.text: **Check**: 32 pieces need 31 breakpoints and a single layer of $k$ nodes has at most $k$ breakpoints, so $k\ge31$. Question 1 is an asymptotic formula, not an exact measurement.

steps.label: Universal approximation
steps.speakerNotes: Level: undergraduate (year 3). Main line 8 pages plus 3 extension pages (not timed). Self-study deck, English version. Made under CLARITY.md C12 to C18. The theorems, the rates O(r^(-2/l)) against O(1/k) and the fixed against adaptive basis explanation follow the source; every number (largest errors of polynomials and sigmoid nets, the Runge phenomenon, the high-dimensional ridge, the random starts, the piece counts of the hat function) was recomputed by a program and these experiments were designed for this lecture (added), and the page states honestly that polynomials are not worse on a smooth one-dimensional target and that the high-dimensional ridge is a design that favours the network. Speaker notes are published with the file and contain no student numbers, grades or exam items.

steps.label: The ticket
steps.speakerNotes: The RBF of KP16 fills the space with local nodes. This page asks which kind of new coordinates can finally approximate any function and which does it fastest. First the universal approximation theorem: with enough nodes, or a high enough order, any continuous function on a compact set can be approximated to any small error; a compact set is bounded and contains its boundary, for example the interval 0 to 1. All three hold: polynomials, which is Weierstrass's theorem, a one-hidden-layer sigmoid network and an RBF network. The real difference lies in how fast the error falls with the order, r to the minus 2 over l for polynomials and 1 over k for sigmoid networks, and in how hard the optimization is. The source calls this the ticket to enter, not an advantage. The next page looks at polynomials first.

steps.label: The polynomial guarantee
steps.speakerNotes: The previous page said all three are universal approximators. This page looks at polynomials first: does the error really keep falling as the order grows? Weierstrass's theorem: for a continuous g on a compact set and any epsilon above 0 there is an order-r polynomial phi whose difference from g is below epsilon. The example was designed here: g equal to sin 2 pi x plus 0.3 x squared on the interval 0 to 1, least squares on 401 points; the largest error for r equal to 1, 3, 5, 7, 9 and 11 is 0.998, 0.198, 0.0152, 0.000607, 0.000015 and 2.5 times 10 to the minus 7. Note that the largest error is the worst point of the whole interval, not an average. The next page asks whether a higher order always fits better.

steps.label: The Runge phenomenon
steps.speakerNotes: The previous page showed the largest error of the polynomial falling steadily with the order. This page asks whether a higher order is always a better fit. First the Runge phenomenon: interpolating a high-order polynomial through equal-spaced points oscillates wildly near the ends and the error grows. Example: g equal to 1 over 1 plus 25 x squared on the interval minus 1 to 1; equal-spaced interpolation at r equal to 4, 8, 12, 16 and 20 has largest error 0.44, 1.05, 3.66, 14.4 and 59.8. Contrast: least squares on 400 points gives 0.33, 0.15, 0.068, 0.031 and 0.014, slow but steady. The source also warns that high-order polynomials suffer from numerical error through many products and from too many free parameters. The next page switches to the sigmoid network.

steps.label: The sigmoid network
steps.speakerNotes: The previous page used the Runge phenomenon to warn about high-order polynomials. This page asks how the largest error depends on the number of nodes with one hidden layer of sigmoids. First the squashing function: a monotonically increasing function that squeezes any input into a bounded range, for example the sigmoid. The theorem: with a squashing activation a one-hidden-layer network with large enough k approximates any continuous function on a compact set to any error. The example uses the target of page 2: k equal to 1, 2, 3, 4, 6 and 8, best of 8 random starts, has largest error 0.819, 0.0142, 0.0056, 0.0058, 0.0045 and 0.0011; two sigmoids already follow the wave. The next page asks who is more accurate, compared with polynomials.

steps.label: A fair test in 1-D
steps.speakerNotes: The previous page said the sigmoid network with k equal to 2 has largest error 0.014. This page asks which is more accurate against a polynomial with the same number of parameters. Honestly: with 7 parameters the polynomial r equal to 6 gives 0.0152 and the sigmoid network k equal to 2, where 3k plus 1 is 7, gives 0.0142, about the same; with 13 parameters the polynomial r equal to 12 gives 2.5 times 10 to the minus 7 while the network k equal to 4 gives 0.0058. So the advantage of the network is not on a smooth one-dimensional target; the rate difference of the theorem shows only in high dimensions. The next page looks at high dimensions.

steps.label: High dimension
steps.speakerNotes: The previous page said the polynomial does not lose in one dimension. This page asks who is more accurate with 5 inputs. The setup was designed here: l equal to 5 standard-normal inputs, the target tanh of 2 times w transpose x, a sigmoid-type function of one direction w, 3000 training points and 2000 new points, with root-mean-square error. Polynomials of r equal to 1, 2, 3 and 5, with 6, 21, 56 and 252 terms, have error 0.326, 0.326, 0.222 and 0.257 on new points; networks with k equal to 1, 2 and 4, with 8, 15 and 29 parameters, are all below 0.0001. An honest note: this target has exactly the shape of the network, a design that favours it, and the normal inputs are unbounded, not a compact set. The next page looks at the rates given by the source.

steps.label: The rates
steps.speakerNotes: The previous page said the polynomial loses in high dimensions while a single network node is almost exact. This page asks what error rates lie behind that. The source cites Barron 93: O of r to the minus 2 over l for polynomials and O of 1 over k for a one-hidden-layer sigmoid network, with the input dimension l absent from the formula. Example: halving the error multiplies the polynomial's r by 2 to the l over 2, which is 2, 5.7, 32 and 1024 times for l equal to 2, 5, 10 and 20, while the network's k only doubles. The limit: these are asymptotic rates, not measurements, and the functions and sizes of k they apply to depend on the conditions of the source and the original paper. The next page asks why the gap is so large and what the price is.

steps.label: Why, and the price
steps.speakerNotes: The previous page said that in the rate formulas the network has no dimension and the polynomial does. This page asks why the gap is so large and what the price is. Two terms first: a fixed basis means basis functions such as x1 squared times x2 that are the same whatever the data look like, which polynomials use; a data-adaptive basis means basis functions f of w transpose x whose w is optimized from the data, which the hidden nodes of a network are. The source says every expansion on a fixed basis is doomed to an error that falls more slowly as the dimension grows. The price is that the optimization turns from linear into nonlinear: for the same data, k equal to 2 with 8 random starts, 5 reach a largest error below 0.1 and 3 get stuck near 0.82, which I computed with a program. The next extension page asks why use more layers if one hidden layer suffices.

steps.label: Extension: depth
steps.speakerNotes: The previous page said the price of the network is a non-convex optimization. This extension asks why use more layers if one hidden layer suffices; enough is not efficient. The hat function h equal to 2 times the smaller of x and 1 minus x takes 2 ReLU nodes; stacking n layers gives 2 to the n straight pieces, which a program counted for n from 1 to 4 as 2, 4, 8 and 16. Number of nodes: 2n when deep; a one-hidden-layer ReLU network has at most k plus 1 pieces and so needs 2 to the n minus 1 nodes. For n equal to 3, 6 and 10: 6, 12 and 20 deep against 7, 63 and 1023 in one layer. The source says more than one hidden layer may reach the same accuracy with fewer neurons. The next page poses an exercise.

steps.label: Extension: practice
steps.speakerNotes: The previous page showed that stacking n hat functions saves many nodes in a deep network over one layer. This page poses an exercise. Question 1: with l equal to 8 and the polynomial error about r to the minus 2 over l, by what factor must r grow to halve the error? Question 2: how many pieces does the five-fold hat function have, and how many ReLU nodes do a deep network and a one-hidden-layer network need? Work it out first, then see the next page.

steps.label: Extension: solution
steps.speakerNotes: The previous page posed the exercise and this page is the complete solution. Question 1: halving r to the minus 2 over 8 needs r times 2 to the 8 over 2, which is 2 to the 4, which is 16. Question 2: 5 layers have 2 to the 5, which is 32 pieces; the deep network needs 2 times 5, which is 10 nodes; one hidden layer needs 2 to the 5 minus 1, which is 31. Check: 32 pieces need 31 breakpoints and a single layer of k nodes has at most k breakpoints, so k must be at least 31; question 1 is an asymptotic formula, not an exact measurement. That finishes the universal approximation theorem; the next knowledge point looks at probabilistic neural networks.

metadata.title: Pattern Recognition, Chapter 4, KP17: the universal approximation theorem, who can approximate any function and how fast (undergraduate, self-study)
